❓ FAQ: AI Total Cost of Ownership

What is AI total cost of ownership?

AI total cost of ownership (TCO) is the full lifetime cost of an AI product across four layers: building it, running it (inference, infrastructure, monitoring), governing it (compliance, security, audit), and the people side (training, change management, workflow redesign).

How much does an enterprise AI product cost?

Gartner estimates generative AI deployments cost between US$5 million and US$20 million depending on approach, with costs less predictable than traditional software. Smaller scoped agentic products can cost far less — if run, governance, and people costs are designed in from day one.

Why do so many AI projects get cancelled?

Gartner predicts over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by end-2027, citing escalating costs, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls. Most failures trace back to pricing the pilot instead of the full cost of ownership.

How can Malaysian companies reduce AI TCO?

Use co-funding like MDEC’s MDAG-AI grant for the build layer, route workloads to smaller models to control inference costs, build governance for PDPA and AIGE from day one, and use a co-build model so capability transfers in-house instead of renting consultants indefinitely.

medium.titulo: System Design Jargons Explained Simply: A Beginner’s Guide
medium.resumo: If you’re a fresher, student, or someone just entering software development, system design can feel intimidating.
medium.conteudo_html:
If you’re a fresher, student, or someone just entering software development, system design can feel intimidating.

You open an interview preparation guide and suddenly encounter:

  • Load Balancer
  • API Gateway
  • Cache
  • CDN
  • Message Queue
  • Database Sharding
  • Horizontal Scaling
  • Vertical Scaling
  • Rate Limiting
  • Microservices

It can feel like everyone is speaking another language.

The good news?

Most system design jargon exists because developers need names for common problems and solutions.

Let’s simplify some of the most common terms.

1. Load Balancer

Imagine you have one server handling 10 users.

Then suddenly 10,000 users arrive.

One server may struggle to handle all those requests.

A load balancer distributes incoming requests across multiple servers.

Users
  |
  v
Load Balancer
 /    |    \
v     v     v
S1    S2    S3

Simple idea

Load Balancer = traffic distributor

It helps prevent one server from receiving all the traffic.

2. Caching

Suppose your application repeatedly needs the same data.

Instead of querying the database every time, you can temporarily store frequently accessed data in a faster storage layer.

That’s caching.

User
 |
 v
Application
 |
 v
Cache -----> Database

If the requested data is already in the cache, the application can retrieve it without making another database query.

Simple idea

Cache = keep frequently needed data nearby

3. API Gateway

Imagine an application has several backend services:

Authentication Service
Payment Service
Order Service
Notification Service

Instead of clients communicating directly with every service, an API Gateway can act as a central entry point.

Client
   |
   v
API Gateway
 /   |    \
Auth Order Payment

Simple idea

API Gateway = front door to backend services

It can also handle things such as routing, authentication-related checks, and rate limiting depending on the architecture.

4. Message Queue

Not every task needs to happen immediately.

Imagine a user uploads a video.

The application could immediately process the video, but that may take time.

Instead, it can place a task into a message queue.

User
 |
 v
Application
 |
 v
Queue
 |
 v
Worker
 |
 v
Video Processing

A worker can process tasks from the queue.

Simple idea

Message Queue = a waiting line for tasks

It helps services communicate asynchronously and can absorb bursts of work.

5. CDN

A Content Delivery Network (CDN) is a distributed network used to deliver content closer to users.

Imagine your main server is located far away from a user.

A CDN can cache eligible content at an edge location closer to that user.

Simple idea

CDN = deliver content from locations closer to users

CDNs are commonly used for assets such as images, CSS, JavaScript, and videos.

6. Horizontal Scaling

Your application is becoming popular.

Instead of relying on one server, you add more servers.

Before:
Server 1
After:
Server 1
Server 2
Server 3
Server 4

This is horizontal scaling.

Simple idea

Horizontal scaling = add more machines

7. Vertical Scaling

There is another approach.

Instead of adding more servers, you make the existing server more powerful.

For example:

  • More RAM
  • More CPU
  • Faster storage

That’s vertical scaling.

Simple idea

Vertical scaling = make one machine stronger

8. Database Sharding

Imagine your database has grown enormously.

Keeping all the data on one database server can become difficult.

Sharding divides data across multiple database instances according to a chosen sharding strategy.

For example:

Database
Shard 1 → Users A–F
Shard 2 → Users G–M
Shard 3 → Users N–S
Shard 4 → Users T–Z

The actual strategy depends on the application.

Simple idea

Sharding = split database data across multiple machines

9. Rate Limiting

Imagine someone sends thousands of requests to your API within a few seconds.

That can consume resources and potentially contribute to abuse.

Rate limiting restricts how many requests a client can make during a defined period.

For example:

100 requests / minute

Simple idea

Rate limiting = control request frequency

10. Microservices

A traditional application might contain many features inside one large application.

With a microservices architecture, functionality can be divided into smaller services.

For example:

Application
                    |
      -----------------------------
      |       |       |           |
    Auth    Orders  Payments   Notifications

Each service can potentially be developed, deployed, and scaled independently.

Simple idea

Microservices = split a large application into smaller services

Microservices aren’t automatically better than a monolith. They introduce their own operational and architectural complexity.

How Should a Fresher Learn System Design?

Don’t start by memorizing 100 terms.

Start with the problem.

Ask yourself:

What problem does this technology or architecture solve?

For example:

Problem: Too many requests are reaching one server.

Possible concept: Load balancing.

Problem: The same data is requested repeatedly.

Possible concept: Caching.

Problem: A long-running task shouldn’t block the user’s request.

Possible concept: Asynchronous processing with a message queue.

Problem: API clients are sending too many requests.

Possible concept: Rate limiting.

This way of thinking is much more useful than memorizing definitions.

A Simple Mental Model

When learning system design, think about five questions:

1. Traffic

How many users and requests are we handling?

2. Storage

Where is our data stored?

3. Performance

How quickly do users need a response?

4. Reliability

What happens if something fails?

5. Scalability

What happens when the application becomes 10x larger?

These questions naturally lead you toward system design concepts.

Final Takeaway

System design isn’t just about complicated diagrams.

It’s about understanding problems, constraints, and trade-offs.

You don’t need to know every architecture as a fresher.

Start with the fundamentals:

Request → Server → Database → Cache → Queue → Scaling → Reliability

Once these concepts become familiar, more advanced system design topics become much easier to understand.

And remember:

Don’t memorize the jargon. Understand the problem behind the jargon.

medium.titulo: How to Use Claude AI as a Personal Tutor
medium.resumo: Learning has traditionally followed a relatively fixed structure: read a lesson, attend a class, complete an exercise, and ask a teacher…
medium.conteudo_html:
Learning has traditionally followed a relatively fixed structure: read a lesson, attend a class, complete an exercise, and ask a teacher or colleague for clarification when something is difficult.

AI assistants are changing that model.

Instead of using AI only to generate answers, learners can use tools such as Claude to explain difficult concepts, create practice exercises, provide feedback, adapt explanations to different levels, and turn passive reading into interactive learning.

Claude can work with uploaded documents and other learning materials, while features such as Projects allow users to organize related knowledge and instructions into focused workspaces. Anthropic also provides guidance for using Claude with research, files, and structured prompts.

For professionals exploring Claude more systematically, the Claude AI Professional E-Degree is one possible learning resource. But the more interesting question is how Claude can actually fit into a learner’s everyday study process.

Used thoughtfully, an AI assistant can become less like an answer machine and more like an on-demand study partner.

The key is to design the interaction around learning, rather than simply obtaining the final answer.

Why an AI Tutor Is Different From a Search Engine

A search engine is excellent at helping you find information.

An AI tutor can take a different role: it can interact with you while you learn.

Suppose you are trying to understand a difficult programming concept.

A search engine might lead you to documentation, tutorials, videos, and forum discussions.

Claude can instead be asked to:

  • Explain the concept at a beginner level
  • Give you an analogy
  • Ask questions to test your understanding
  • Provide a practice problem
  • Review your answer
  • Explain where your reasoning went wrong
  • Increase the difficulty gradually

This creates a feedback loop.

Learn → Practice → Receive feedback → Try again

That loop is much closer to active learning than simply reading an explanation.

Start by Defining Your Learning Goal

One of the biggest mistakes people make with AI learning is starting with a vague request.

For example:

“Teach me Python.”

Python is a huge subject.

A better request defines a specific outcome:

“I want to understand Python functions well enough to read and modify simple programs. Assume I know variables and basic loops. Teach me through short explanations followed by practice questions.”

This gives Claude information about:

  • Your current level
  • Your goal
  • What you already know
  • What you want to learn
  • How you want to learn

Anthropic’s prompting guidance recommends being clear and direct, providing context, and specifying the desired output rather than expecting the model to infer all of these details.

The principle applies beyond Claude.

The better the learning objective, the more useful the tutoring interaction becomes.

Ask Claude to Teach at Your Level

The same topic can require completely different explanations depending on the learner.

Consider the concept of APIs.

A beginner might need an explanation using a restaurant analogy.

A developer might want to discuss HTTP methods, authentication, status codes, and request/response structures.

An experienced engineer might want to compare REST with GraphQL or event-driven architectures.

Instead of asking Claude:

“Explain APIs.”

tell it where you are starting.

For example:

“Explain REST APIs to someone who understands basic JavaScript but has never built a backend service. Start with the mental model before introducing technical terminology.”

You can then progressively increase the difficulty.

This makes the conversation adaptive rather than forcing the learner through a fixed explanation.

Use the Socratic Method

One of the most useful ways to prevent AI from doing all the thinking for you is to ask it to behave like a tutor rather than an answer generator.

The Socratic method works by using questions to guide understanding.

For example, instead of:

“What is the difference between a list and a tuple in Python?”

ask:

“Teach me lists and tuples using questions. Don’t reveal the answer immediately. Ask me one question at a time and correct my reasoning when necessary.”

The interaction might then progress from a simple question to a more difficult one.

This is valuable because the learner has to retrieve and apply information rather than simply recognize a correct explanation.

A useful instruction is:

“If I make a mistake, don’t immediately give me the complete answer. Give me a hint first.”

That small change can make an AI conversation much more educational.

Turn Reading Into Active Learning

Reading a chapter or article can create the feeling that you understand something without actually testing whether you can use it.

Claude can help turn reading into an active exercise.

After studying a topic, provide the relevant material and ask:

“Create five questions that test whether I actually understand this material. Include two conceptual questions, two application questions, and one question that requires identifying a common misconception.”

Then answer the questions without looking back at the source.

Afterward, ask Claude to evaluate your responses.

This creates a simple cycle:

Read → Recall → Apply → Receive feedback

That is more useful than repeatedly rereading the same material.

Don’t Ask for the Answer Too Quickly

AI makes it extremely easy to bypass difficult parts of learning.

Suppose you are working on a mathematics problem.

You could ask:

“Solve this.”

Claude may provide the complete solution within seconds.

That can be useful when checking work, but it is not necessarily useful when learning.

Instead, try:

“Give me the first hint only. Don’t solve the problem.”

If you still need help:

“Give me a second hint.”

Finally:

“Now show me the complete solution and explain where my approach went wrong.”

This creates a progression from independent problem-solving toward guided assistance.

The objective is not to make AI less capable.

It is to make the learner more capable.

Create Personalized Practice Tests

Once Claude knows what you are studying, it can help create practice material.

For example, a learner preparing for a technical interview might ask for:

  • Multiple-choice questions
  • Short-answer questions
  • Scenario-based questions
  • Coding exercises
  • Troubleshooting situations
  • Conceptual questions

A professional studying business analytics could request exercises based on realistic workplace scenarios.

Someone learning a language could practice vocabulary, grammar, translation, and conversation.

The important part is to specify the difficulty.

Instead of:

“Give me JavaScript questions.”

try:

“Create 10 intermediate JavaScript questions. Focus on asynchronous programming, promises, closures, and error handling. Don’t provide answers until I submit mine.”

This makes the AI behave more like an assessment tool.

Ask Claude to Find Your Weak Areas

Another useful approach is to use repeated practice to identify patterns.

After answering several questions, ask:

“Review my answers and identify the three concepts I appear to misunderstand most. For each one, explain the misconception and give me one short exercise.”

This turns individual mistakes into a learning plan.

For example, a learner might discover that they understand JavaScript syntax but repeatedly struggle with asynchronous execution.

Instead of continuing to study JavaScript broadly, they can focus specifically on that gap.

This is where AI tutoring can become personalized.

Use Your Own Learning Materials

Generic explanations are useful, but your actual course material may use particular terminology, frameworks, or examples.

Claude can work with supported document formats including PDFs, DOCX, CSV, TXT, HTML, JSON, and other formats, subject to the applicable limits and features.

That means a learner can potentially build study sessions around material they are already expected to understand.

For example:

“Use this chapter as the primary source for the quiz. Ask questions only about concepts covered in the material.”

This can be especially useful when preparing for an examination or professional certification.

It also reduces the problem of studying material that is unrelated to the actual curriculum.

However, important facts should still be checked against the original source, particularly when accuracy matters.

Build a Study Project

For a longer course, organizing everything into a single learning environment can make the process more consistent.

Claude Projects allow users to create focused workspaces with project-specific knowledge and instructions. Documents, code, and other relevant material can be added to the project’s knowledge base, while project instructions can define how Claude should behave across conversations.

A learner could create a project such as:

“Data Analytics Study Plan”

The knowledge base might include:

  • Course notes
  • Reference PDFs
  • Glossaries
  • Practice material
  • Assignment instructions
  • Personal notes

Project instructions could say:

“Act as a patient tutor. Explain unfamiliar concepts before using advanced terminology. When I make an error, give me a hint before providing the answer. Use examples based on the supplied course material whenever possible.”

The learner could then have separate conversations for different topics while maintaining a consistent learning environment.

Ask for Multiple Explanations

Sometimes the problem is not that a concept is difficult.

The explanation is simply not compatible with the way you currently understand the subject.

When that happens, ask Claude to explain the same idea differently.

For example:

“Explain recursion using a visual mental model.”

Then:

“Explain it using a real-world analogy.”

Then:

“Now explain it technically as if I were preparing for a developer interview.”

Different explanations can expose different aspects of the same concept.

You can also ask Claude to identify the misconception preventing you from understanding the topic.

Use Claude for Feedback, Not Just Answers

Writing is another area where personalized AI feedback can be useful.

A learner can submit an essay, technical explanation, presentation outline, or professional email and ask Claude to evaluate it against specific criteria.

For example:

“Evaluate this explanation for clarity, logical structure, technical accuracy, and unnecessary jargon. Don’t rewrite it yet. First explain what I should improve.”

This is often more educational than immediately asking for a polished rewrite.

The learner can then make the changes themselves.

Afterward, Claude can perform another review.

This creates:

Draft → Feedback → Revision → Second review

rather than:

Draft → AI rewrite → Finished

The first process develops the learner’s own ability.

Learn by Building Small Projects

Knowledge becomes much more useful when it can be applied.

Suppose you have learned basic HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

Instead of asking Claude to build an entire website for you, ask it to help you design a small project that tests the concepts you have learned.

For example:

“Give me a small project that requires DOM manipulation, event handling, and local data storage. Don’t provide the implementation. Give me requirements and milestones.”

You can then build the project yourself.

When you get stuck, ask for a hint rather than the complete solution.

Claude can review your approach, explain errors, and suggest what to investigate next.

This preserves the most valuable part of project-based learning: actually solving problems.

Be Careful With AI-Generated Explanations

AI tutoring has an important limitation.

An AI can produce an explanation that sounds convincing even when part of it is incorrect.

This is particularly important for:

  • Mathematics
  • Programming
  • Scientific concepts
  • Law
  • Medicine
  • Finance
  • Current events

For important subjects, use primary sources, textbooks, official documentation, instructors, and other authoritative resources to verify critical information.

Claude’s research functionality can help gather and synthesize information with citations when web search is enabled, but citations should still be checked against their underlying sources.

AI can accelerate learning, but it should not remove the learner’s responsibility to evaluate information.

Avoid Turning Learning Into Prompt Copying

There is another subtle problem with AI-assisted education: learners can become good at prompting without becoming good at the subject.

For example, someone may repeatedly ask:

“Explain this.”

“Summarize this.”

“Give me the answer.”

“Rewrite this.”

They may produce polished results while retaining little understanding.

A stronger learning workflow asks the AI to make you participate.

Use prompts such as:

“Quiz me.”

“Give me a problem without the solution.”

“Ask me why.”

“Challenge my reasoning.”

“Find the weakest part of my explanation.”

“Give me a hint instead of the answer.”

These prompts shift Claude from a content generator toward a learning partner.

A Simple Claude Study Routine

You can build a practical study session around five stages.

1. Learn

Ask Claude to explain the concept at your current level.

2. Test

Ask for questions without answers.

3. Apply

Solve a problem or complete a small task independently.

4. Review

Give Claude your answer and ask for feedback based on explicit criteria.

5. Reflect

Ask:

“What should I study next based on the mistakes I made today?”

This creates a continuous feedback loop.

For a longer course, keep a record of recurring mistakes and topics that still feel unclear. That record can become the basis for future study sessions.

The Bigger Idea: AI Should Support Learning, Not Replace It

The most useful role for Claude in education may not be giving faster answers.

It may be making high-quality feedback and practice more accessible.

A learner can ask for another explanation without worrying about interrupting a class. They can practice at their own pace, request easier or harder examples, and receive feedback on preliminary work.

But the responsibility for learning still belongs to the learner.

The best AI-assisted study habits preserve the difficult parts of learning: remembering, questioning, solving, explaining, making mistakes, and trying again.

That is what turns an AI assistant from a shortcut into a learning tool.

Final Thoughts

Claude can support many stages of learning, from understanding a new concept to testing knowledge, reviewing mistakes, and designing practical projects.

The strongest approach is not to ask Claude to do the learning for you. Instead, use it to create a more interactive learning environment: ask questions, challenge your assumptions, request hints, practice without answers, and verify important information against reliable sources.

For professionals interested in developing a more structured understanding of Claude and its practical applications, the Claude AI Professional E-Degree is one resource worth exploring alongside hands-on practice.

The most valuable skill is learning how to work with AI without surrendering your own thinking. When Claude explains, questions, challenges, and provides feedback while you remain responsible for understanding the material, AI becomes less of an answer generator and more of a flexible study partner.

medium.titulo: Introducing Nuxt Native v1 — Developer Preview
medium.resumo: Build truly native mobile apps with Vue and the Nuxt developer experience, powered by NativeScript.
medium.conteudo_html:
Build truly native mobile apps with Vue and the Nuxt developer experience, powered by NativeScript.

Today, we’re introducing the developer preview of Nuxt Native — an open-source framework for building native mobile applications using Vue and familiar Nuxt conventions.

If you already love building with Nuxt, Nuxt Native aims to make mobile development feel familiar too.

Instead of rendering your application inside a WebView, Nuxt Native uses NativeScript to render real native UI on Android and iOS.

With Nuxt Native, we’re bringing familiar ideas from the Nuxt ecosystem to native development:

  • Vue Single File Components
  • File-based routing
  • Nuxt-style composables
  • Native UI components
  • Pinia support
  • Native device APIs
  • Simple CLI and developer tooling

This is just the beginning.

Repo:

https://github.com/vastx-tech/nuxt-native

Nuxt Native is currently in Developer Preview, and there is still a lot to build, improve, and explore. We’re releasing early so developers can try it, experiment with it, contribute, and help shape its future.

Our goal is simple:

Make native mobile development feel natural for Vue and Nuxt developers.

Welcome to Nuxt Native. 🚀

medium.titulo: SPA (React/Vue) vs. htmx: Why Towami Chose a Document-First Frontend
medium.resumo: A marketplace page should arrive as usable HTML — for search engines, modern laptops, and mid-range phones on mobile networks.
medium.conteudo_html:
A marketplace page should arrive as usable HTML — for search engines, modern laptops, and mid-range phones on mobile networks.

React and Vue are excellent tools. We chose a different architecture for Towami’s public catalog and merchant storefronts because of the product’s requirements, not because JavaScript frameworks are inherently slow or bad for SEO.

Where React and Vue are the right choice

When the product is primarily an application — a design tool, trading terminal, collaborative editor, or state-heavy dashboard — a component framework and client runtime are often the most productive choice.

The ecosystems are mature, the development model is widely understood, and frameworks such as Next.js and Nuxt can return fully rendered HTML from the server. A React or Vue application is not automatically a client-only SPA, nor is it automatically bad for search.

Shopify illustrates why the distinction matters. Its standard theme stack is an excellent default for many merchants, with mature commerce tooling and broad app compatibility. Shopify Markets supports localized languages, currencies, pricing, and domains. For teams that need a custom headless storefront and already work in React, Hydrogen is also a strong option.

Those are rational choices. Towami’s requirements simply led to a different trade-off.

The boundary we have

Towami has two closely connected public surfaces:

  • country marketplaces across nine markets, with localized English and Spanish routes;
  • white-label merchant storefronts, including storefronts on merchants’ own domains.

Organic search is an important acquisition channel. That means some filter combinations are more than temporary UI state: when they have live inventory, they become indexable landing pages.

For example:

https://cr.towami.com/en/vehicles/cars/for-sale/sedan

That URL needs to return a complete document with a canonical URL, structured data, localized metadata, and — when the combination is eligible — a sitemap entry. It should not exist only after a client-side router has started.

A client-heavy architecture could meet those requirements. But it would add another layer that must remain consistent with the server: routes, locales, currencies, canonical rules, cache variants, and the initial document received by crawlers.

We decided that Towami did not need that layer on its public surfaces.

What the browser receives

Towami’s public UI is rendered by Go using Templ templates.

Browser-side behavior uses htmx, Alpine.js, and a project-specific JavaScript bundle:

  • htmx requests and replaces HTML fragments;
  • Alpine manages local state such as mobile menus, confirmation dialogs, galleries, and checkout options;
  • the site bundle handles behavior that does not fit cleanly into either library.

Navigation is boosted at the <body> level. Ordinary internal links can replace #main-content and update browser history without replacing the entire document. The header remains mounted, with out-of-band updates where its content needs to change.

The initial catalog content arrives as server-rendered HTML. There is no React or Vue hydration step. After an htmx update, Alpine initializes behavior on the new DOM.

Critical CSS for public pages is inlined, while the remaining styles are loaded from separate bundles. Account pages use linked stylesheets because their first render is not an organic-search landing surface.

The largest browser-side dependency is TipTap. It is loaded only in merchant content editors — for products, pages, blog posts, and categories — not in the public catalog.

One URL, two navigation modes

Catalog filters are where this architecture becomes especially useful.

Suppose a visitor selects “sedan.” The filter form uses GET.

For an htmx request, the server:

  1. returns 200 OK;
  2. renders the catalog fragment;
  3. sends HX-Push-Url with the preferred path.

The list updates and the address bar becomes:

/en/vehicles/cars/for-sale/sedan

For an ordinary request — including a browser without JavaScript — the same query-string URL receives a 302 redirect to the preferred path.

There is no crawler detection. The server only distinguishes an htmx request from a regular HTTP request.

Canonical URLs remove non-SEO filters such as price ranges. One allowlisted feature can become the final path segment; additional features remain in ?features=. Sitemap generation only publishes combinations supported by live catalog data.

This gives enhanced navigation to browsers that support it while keeping the underlying links and forms functional without JavaScript.

Keeping response variants separate

A full document and an htmx fragment can share a URL while containing different HTML. The cache must not confuse them.

Towami’s primary full-page and htmx navigation responses use a weak ETag calculated from the rendered body and return:

Vary: Accept, HX-Request, X-Catalog-More
Cache-Control: private, no-cache, must-revalidate

Because the full document, navigation fragment, and “show more” fragment have different bodies, they receive different ETags. A matching conditional request returns 304 Not Modified.

We do not attach a public millisecond claim to this mechanism. The relevant architectural property is simpler: the first response contains the page, while enhanced navigation uses the same URL model instead of creating a second client-only route space.

What we gave up

This approach has costs.

We gave up the standardized React/Vue client-component ecosystem, shared frontend language across server and browser, and the tooling built around large client-side applications.

The merchant interface is also server-rendered. Initial requests return complete Templ pages; subsequent navigation can replace #main-content with htmx fragments. A server-backed interaction usually means implementing a handler that returns markup rather than designing a JSON API and client store.

That model is less attractive for dense interfaces with extensive client state.

We also do not try to turn every transition into app-style navigation. Authentication links and several other flows deliberately perform normal document navigation. Progressive enhancement is a default, not a requirement that every request must be asynchronous.

When we would choose React or Vue

We would choose a client framework if Towami’s primary interface became a real-time operations console, visual page builder, collaborative editor, or another product where most meaningful state lives in the browser.

That would justify the runtime and client-side state model. The public catalog and merchant storefront could still remain document-first.

Modern React and Vue frameworks can also reduce client cost through server components, selective hydration, lazy hydration, and hybrid rendering. The trade-off is therefore one of degree, not an absolute limitation of those technologies.

For Towami, the remaining client-side requirements were small enough that adopting a full application runtime for every public page did not provide enough value.

Performance is a target, not a slogan

Core Web Vitals are among the signals used by Google’s ranking systems, although good scores do not guarantee rankings. Across ecommerce, faster experiences often correlate with better conversion — but that is something each product should measure, not promise in advance.

Towami’s engineering target is a high PageSpeed score and good Core Web Vitals on merchant storefronts. It is not an unconditional guarantee for every page or every uploaded image.

The architecture makes that target more achievable:

  • compiled server-side templates;
  • usable HTML in the initial response;
  • inlined critical CSS;
  • limited JavaScript on public pages;
  • no application-framework hydration;
  • one URL model for visitors and crawlers.

React and Vue remain excellent choices for products that behave primarily as applications. Towami’s public catalog is document-first, with interactivity added where it provides clear value.

corrida_no_ar.resumo: Finalmente sabemos quando abrem as inscrições da São Silvestre! Veja também como o app Runna ajusta seus treinos, a lesão de Bekele, a pintura do Adios Pro 5 descascando e o novo Mizuno de 96g. Além disso, confira a análise completa do Hoka Clifton 11.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Sexta-feira | 25 de setembro de 2026

Finalmente, foi anunciada a data de abertura das inscrições para a 101ª Corrida Internacional de São Silvestre. A venda para o público geral começa na quarta-feira, dia 30 de setembro, a partir das 10h da manhã. O processo mudou: antes, nos dias 24 e 25 de setembro, abre o período para o envio de laudos de comprovação para pessoas com deficiência (PCD). A partir do dia 7 de outubro, também às 10h, será a vez das assessorias, grupos e agências de turismo. As inscrições serão feitas no novo ambiente da Ticket Sports by Ingresse. A recomendação é já deixar o pré-cadastro pronto no site oficial, o saosilvestre.com.br, para agilizar o processo.

O que acontece quando você “fura” o treino no Runna?

Uma das funcionalidades mais interessantes do aplicativo de treinos Runna é sua capacidade de adaptação. Caso você não consiga cumprir as metas propostas, o aplicativo reconhece e sugere um ajuste no plano. Ao perceber que o usuário completou apenas uma parte do treino longo, por exemplo, o Runna exibe uma mensagem como “Vamos analisar a distância do seu plano” e oferece a opção de “Revisar distância”.
